title: Hourglass labour: Employment growth can block progression
desc: Links occupational hollowing to insecurity, skills mismatch and weak mobility, distinguishing job quantity from job quality and productivity.

kps.k: An hourglass labour market can sustain employment growth while weakening job quality and routes into better-paid work.
kps.d: The London Assembly Economy Committee’s February 2016 report examines London mainly over 2008–2015, drawing on commissioned GLA Economics analysis, statistics, surveys and witness evidence. Employment rose from 71% to 73% and unemployment fell from 8% to 6%, but the Committee argues that these gains concealed problems in progression, pay, security and productivity. Its hourglass describes the erosion of mid-skilled occupations across London’s economy—not law-firm staffing or evidence of generative-AI displacement.

qs.q: The  unemployment rate reached its lowest ever level in 2015, down from eight to  six per cent over the period, while the employment rate increased from 71 to  73 per cent,2 resulting in a greater proportion of the population in  employment than before the economic downturn.
qs.a: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market · Regulators & courts · 2016

kps.k: The report links occupational hollowing-out to blocked progression, but offers qualified explanations rather than a demonstrated single cause of weak productivity.
kps.d: Between 2008 and 2015, high-skilled jobs increased from 51% to 53% of workforce jobs, while the mid-skilled share fell from approximately 20% to 18%; the report describes the latter as a 13% relative decline. The Committee argues that losing administrative, manufacturing and trade roles restricted upward mobility. It treats skills shortages as a partial explanation for London’s slower productivity growth than the UK’s over 2008–2013. Separately, Ian Brinkley argues that abundant cheap labour reduced incentives to automate, while the report presents workforce composition, weak progression and skills investment as further hypotheses.

qs.q: Productivity  Between 2008 and 2013, productivity, the measure of output per worker,  grew at a slower rate than the rest of the UK.3 This appears, to some extent at  least, to be tied to a skills shortage in the labour market.
qs.a: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market · Regulators & courts · 2016

qs.q: 10    1.3  During our investigation, we heard from Ian Brinkley, of the Work Foundation,  that the reason the relative number of lower skilled jobs in London increased  from 2008 to 2015 was that the availability of lots of cheap labour during the  recession removed the need for workforce efficiencies to be made, through  automation and technology.
qs.a: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market · Regulators & courts · 2016

kps.k: Employer evidence points to skills mismatch, not simply a shortage of jobs or older workers obstructing younger entrants.
kps.d: The report cites the CBI’s 2015 survey, in which 55% of employers lacked confidence that they could recruit enough high-skilled employees, alongside a forecast that most jobs created during 2012–2022 would be high-skilled. These are expectations, not observed outcomes for that decade. The Committee identifies indications of declining training investment and inadequate adult careers advice despite strong school results. It rejects older-worker displacement as the explanation for young people’s difficulties, instead reporting employer concerns about workplace skills and experience.

qs.q: The CBI, in their 2015 annual education and skills  survey, found that “Most jobs created in the decade 2012-2022 are expected  to be high-skilled ones.” Yet, 55 per cent of employers surveyed are “not  confident of being able to recruit sufficient high-skilled employees in future.”  1.10 As we heard from the Greater London Authority:  “The skill system is behind the times.
qs.a: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market · Regulators & courts · 2016

qs.q: Separately, there  are indications that investment in basic workplace skills and training,  including in formal education, has declined.
qs.a: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market · Regulators & courts · 2016

kps.k: Employment-preserving flexibility carried uneven costs, especially for workers needing secure, part-time work.
kps.d: The report says employers protected jobs through reduced hours, casualisation and frozen pay. Part-time jobs grew by 23% after the recession, compared with 9% for full-time jobs. The Committee distinguishes beneficial, well-paid flexibility from insecure arrangements: only 3% of advertised London jobs above £20,000 full-time equivalent offered part-time work or flexibility. In 2015, 24% of female employee jobs and 49% of jobs held by 18–24-year-olds paid below the London Living Wage, against 17% of male employee jobs. Across London, the share below that threshold rose by 54% during 2008–2015. The Committee connects stagnant wages and rising living costs with greater in-work poverty risk.

qs.q: Following the 2008 global financial services  crash, employment in London – and across the rest of the country – remained  buoyant, with businesses responding to the downturn by reducing hours,  introducing greater casualisation, and freezing pay in order to protect jobs.
qs.a: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market · Regulators & courts · 2016

qs.q: The proportion employed on such contracts increased  from 25 to 29 per cent between 2008 and 2015.6   Although qualityb, well-paid flexible working can be of great benefit to  workers, particularly those with caring responsibilities, there are indications  that flexible arrangements designed with the worker in mind were few during  the downturn and have seen limited improvement since.
qs.a: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market · Regulators & courts · 2016

kps.k: The policy disagreement concerns what counts as success and how far public intervention should extend.
kps.d: The Committee challenges the mayoral team’s emphasis on job and apprenticeship totals and calls for rigorous job-quality measures, including the number of workers receiving the London Living Wage rather than accredited employer counts. It acknowledges limited mayoral powers and welcomes apprenticeship initiatives. Its proposals combine sector-tailored training, adult advancement support, clearer contracts, fairer conditions and flexible hiring through public employment and procurement. It supports wider Living Wage coverage but asks for analysis of job creation and losses before considering a mandate by 2020. It also predicts that devolved funding would improve employment support and skilled-job creation; these remain proposed benefits, not evaluated results.

qs.q: Furthermore, the current Mayor,  and his advisors have repeatedly prioritised the number of full-time jobs,  part-time jobs, and apprenticeships created in the capital, and have neglected  to stress the importance of the quality of those jobs.
qs.a: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market · Regulators & courts · 2016

qs.q: 5.4  The Mayoralty has few economic levers which can be employed to steer the  development of London’s labour market.
qs.a: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market · Regulators & courts · 2016

vlens.an: The London Assembly Economy Committee directly supports the proposition that employment growth can coexist with an hourglass labour market that weakens job quality and progression. Its principal reasons are that favourable headline employment figures in London during 2008–2015 concealed declining mid-skilled employment, restricted routes from low-paid work into better-paid roles, greater casualisation and part-time work, wage pressure, and skills mismatch. The report also argues that labour-market success should be assessed through pay, security, skills development, career mobility and productivity rather than job totals alone. Material internal variation lies mainly in the strength of its causal and policy claims: occupational hollowing and blocked progression are presented firmly, but skills shortages are only a partial explanation for weak productivity; other mechanisms are attributed as hypotheses or witness views. Likewise, Living Wage mandates and devolution benefits are proposals requiring analysis, not demonstrated outcomes. This assessment concerns this curated committee report and should not be generalized to all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: We have found that, when the full picture is taken into account, London has  performed less well against these factors, between 2008 and 2015, than the  headline figures might suggest.
qs.a: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market · Regulators & courts · 2016

elens.an: The 2016 London Assembly report directly supports the proposition that employment growth can coexist with—and conceal—an hourglass labour market marked by poorer job quality and blocked progression. For London over 2008–2015, it contrasts improving headline employment and unemployment figures with weaker outcomes in pay, security, skills, productivity and career mobility. Its central mechanism is occupational hollowing: the declining share of mid-skilled administrative, manufacturing and trade jobs reduced pathways from low-paid work into better-paid, higher-skilled roles and enlarged the available low-paid labour pool. The report also adds important qualification. It does not establish automation as the cause of the hollowing; instead, it reports an argument that abundant cheap labour reduced firms’ incentives to automate. Likewise, skills shortages, weak training investment and poor progression are presented as partial or proposed explanations for weak productivity rather than a demonstrated single cause. Because this time-period facet contains one curated source, the finding characterises that source’s position and should not be treated as evidence of broader prevalence.
